title: Do. One. Thing.
author: Andrew Ellison
summary: Ellison takes Socrates' description of democracy in Republic VIII as a general store full of pretty wares and turns it into a diagnosis of academic leadership in classical schools. Teachers and headmasters now face an effectively unlimited menu of curricula, methods, books, and professional development options, and that abundance does not liberate them but paralyzes them. His categorical counsel is to choose one thing and do it well for years, building what he calls institutional craft knowledge strong enough to survive annual staff turnover. He applies the principle to whole faculty liberal learning, arguing that letting teachers self select into interest groups fragments a faculty into cliques and squanders the culture building power of everyone reading the same text together, with Euclid offered as the bracing example. Two cautionary cases follow: Latin teachers whose pursuit of the mythical best curriculum leaves students restarting the language three years running, and a Humane Letters teacher whose sweeping course redesign had to be refused with the line that the course is the measure of the teacher, not the teacher of the course. Ellison closes by placing the burden squarely on school leaders to resist tinkering, refuse expensive textbook churn, and hold grade and subject teams tightly coordinated on fundamentals. The piece is unusual in treating curricular restlessness as a leadership failure rather than a sign of vitality.
points: The governing analogy is Plato's general store: an abundance of good options produces aimlessness rather than excellence, in schools as in a democratic city.
Ellison wants faculty development to repeat rather than rotate, so that a school accumulates decentralized craft knowledge that outlasts the people who leave.
He argues that offering teachers a choice of professional reading groups actively fragments a faculty, and prescribes one shared text for everyone instead.
He names tinkeritis curricularis as a recurring institutional disease, illustrated by a cohort receiving three different Latin curricula in three consecutive years.
His defense of a fixed course against individual academic freedom rests on an educators' consensus stretching back decades rather than the interests of the teacher in the room.
quotes: In Book VIII of the Republic (557c-d), Socrates offers an interesting account of the nature of democracy, characterizing it as the “prettiest” sort of regime, “like a general store”, containing all sorts of interesting wares and multi-colored things to choose from.
This is no good thing for the soul, he goes on to argue, for the infinite choices and wide freedoms of life in a democratic city beget a certain type of aimlessness and lack of purpose.

When faced with so many choices about curriculum, textbooks, methods, and professional development, my categorical guidance for teachers and school leaders is: choose ONE thing and do it well. Stick with that one thing. Do it again and again, and get good at it.
For education and culture-building require constancy of purpose and methods. Variety, novelty, and experimentation will always stop your efforts dead in their tracks.
But this cafeteria-style approach doesn’t build focus and purpose amongst faculty. Its effect is to pull teachers apart into separate cliques.

When this passion for perfection isn’t reined in by the headmaster at the school level, the unfortunate result will be a disjointed and discontinuous experience for the students as they ascend from grade to grade.

School leaders, it is up to you and you alone to maintain academic and cultural focus, unity, and coherence in your school. You are the safeguard of this principle and no one else. Resist pressure to tinker, experiment, or mix it up.
And insist upon the tightest unity and focus upon the things that matter most in your schools: the culture and vision of liberal teaching and learning.
